meta.title: Who really said "Gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all others"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Cicero did call gratitude the mother of all virtues in Pro Plancio (54 BCE) — but this exact English one-liner is a modern paraphrase, not a standard translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all others'?
meta.ogDescription: The thought is genuinely Cicero's (Pro Plancio 80), but the popular English wording is a 20th-century paraphrase of older public-domain translations.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 106 BCE – 43 BCE · Roman statesman, orator & philosopher
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Cicero’s: in Pro Plancio (54 BCE) he tells the jurors that of all virtues he most wishes to be grateful, “for this one virtue is not only the greatest but also the mater virtutum omnium reliquarum” — the mother of all the other virtues (Pro Plancio 33.80 ↗). But this exact English one-liner is a modern paraphrase: standard translations render the subject as “this one virtue” (Yonge) or “a grateful mind” (Ramage, 1884), not “Gratitude,” and the popular wording is first documented only in the 20th century.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Pro Plancio (In Defence of Cn. Plancius)
C. D. Yonge (“the parent of all the other virtues”)

source.excerpt: Etenim, iudices, cum omnibus virtutibus me adfectum esse cupio, tum nihil est quod malim quam me et esse gratum et videri. Haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum. — “In truth, O judges, while I wish to be adorned with every virtue, yet there is nothing which I can esteem more highly than being and appearing grateful. For this one virtue is not only the greatest, but is also the parent of all the other virtues.”
trail: Cicero delivered the Pro Plancio in 54 BCE, defending Cn. Plancius against a charge of electoral corruption; the gratitude passage sits at Pro Plancio 33.80 ↗.

The literal Latin — mater virtutum omnium reliquarum — means ‘mother of all the remaining virtues’; C. D. Yonge rendered it “the parent of all the other virtues” in his public-domain translation (Yonge translation ↗).

The exact popular one-liner is a 20th-century tightening: Wikiquote ↗ lists it as a variant translation traced to a 1950 periodical, alongside Craufurd Tait Ramage’s 1884 “A grateful mind is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all the other virtues.”
source.excerptNote: Cicero’s “this one virtue” (haec una virtus) points back to being grateful (gratum) — which is why the line is universally quoted as being about gratitude, even though the noun “gratitude” itself is supplied by later paraphrasers.
source.rightsNote: The underlying passage is Cicero’s Pro Plancio 80, in the public domain since antiquity. The exact English one-liner is a lightly modernized form of pre-1931, public-domain renderings — C. D. Yonge’s (“the parent of all the other virtues”) and Craufurd Tait Ramage’s 1884 “A grateful mind is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all the other virtues.” The trivial word-swaps in the popular version add no new copyrightable authorship, so the wording is treated as public domain.

author.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.heading: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE) was Rome’s most celebrated orator and a prolific writer on rhetoric, ethics, and politics whose Latin prose shaped European thought for two millennia. The Pro Plancio is one of his surviving forensic speeches, delivered in 54 BCE to defend his friend Cn. Plancius. His reflections on gratitude, duty, and the virtues run throughout his court speeches and philosophical works such as De Officiis.

misattribution.heading: Misquote, not misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a case of accurate attribution but loose wording. The idea is authentically Cicero’s; the polished English sentence is a paraphrase, not any scholar’s translation.

items.why: The thought is his own, from Pro Plancio 80 (54 BCE): “Haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum” (Perseus ↗).

items.who: A modern paraphrase, not a standard translation
items.why: No scholarly translation reads “Gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all others.” Yonge has “this one virtue… the parent of all the other virtues”; Ramage’s 1884 Great Thoughts from Latin Authors has “A grateful mind…” The exact popular form is traced only to a 1950 periodical (Wikiquote ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the wisdom is really Cicero’s, drawn straight from Pro Plancio 80, but the crisp one-liner is a 20th-century paraphrase of older public-domain renderings — so credit the thought to Cicero while noting the wording is not his exact translated text (Pro Plancio 33.80 ↗).

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The line is genuinely rooted in a Roman courtroom, not a book of maxims. Defending Cn. Plancius — who had sheltered Cicero during his exile — Cicero made his own gratitude the emotional core of the defence, arguing that to repay a benefactor is not merely decent but the root from which every other virtue grows.

That is why the thought has traveled so far: it elevates gratitude from a courtesy to a foundation. The catch for quoters is that the crisp modern sentence is a paraphrase — Cicero never wrote the word “gratitude” as the grammatical subject; translators and later editors supplied it.
context.pull: For this one virtue is not only the greatest, but is also the parent of all the other virtues.
